title: The Garden of Forking Paths
scopeNote: This is the forking-paths half of the original activity. The family-wise error rate simulation, the Bonferroni correction and its cost, and the vignette classification stay in the longer version, and the page says so.
summary: One fictional dataset of 90 students generated with no group difference on anything, and four defensible analysis choices over it giving 72 complete reportable analyses. The learner walks a few paths, gets a real p-value from each, and then sees every path they did not take.
learningObjectives: Explain what a p-value is a statement about, and why that statement depends on the analysis having been specified in advance.
Recognise that a single reported analysis can be one of many that were available, without anyone having run the others.
Explain why the analyst need not have acted in bad faith for the reported p-value to be misleading.
Say why paths that share participants and outcomes cannot be handled by a simple correction.
Identify pre-registration and reporting the analysis space as responses to the problem.
interactionTypes: guided movement through four real analysis decisions
a genuine two-sample t-test computed for every path walked
a recorded trail of the analyses the learner ran
withheld reveal of all 72 paths at once, with those walked marked
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every analysis is computed in the browser and the trail is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with every analysis choice a labelled native select. Each result is reported as text giving the p-value, the sample size and the difference in points, and the trail of analyses run is an ordered list rather than only a graphic. The reveal figure carries a description stating how many of the 72 analyses fall below 0.05, how many the learner walked and that the data contain no difference, so the counts do not depend on reading the dots. Walked paths differ from the rest by size and fill as well as by colour. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated. The 90 students, their group assignment, their four outcomes, their baseline score, their working speed and their year of study are all generated in the browser from a fixed seed. Group is assigned independently of every measured variable, so there is no difference to find on any outcome, in any subgroup, under any exclusion rule, adjusted or not.
simulationNotes: Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals, so every learner sees the same dataset. One latent tendency drives all four outcomes and the baseline score, so the outcomes are correlated with each other and with the baseline as real measures on the same people are, and the paths are correspondingly correlated. Each path filters rows by subgroup and exclusion rule, optionally residualises the outcome on the baseline score, and runs a pooled two-sample t-test with a proper Student's t distribution. The seed was chosen by sweeping candidates: it puts 7 of the 72 paths below 0.05 with a smallest p of 0.008, which is enough to look publishable without looking rigged. That exact count is a property of this one simulated sample.
readmeTopic: researcher degrees of freedom, and what choosing an analysis after seeing the data does to a p-value
